name: Armand-Jean du Plessis, duc de Richelieu
role: Chief minister to Louis XIII of France (1624–1642)
summary: Richelieu strengthened royal authority against the military power of the Huguenots and the independence of powerful nobles. He treated Catholic religion as a foundation of government at home and pursued alliances abroad to counter the Habsburgs.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Richelieu recounts in part I, chapter I of the Testament politique how the government deployed its army to secure French positions in northern Italy and defeat the armed rebellion in Languedoc.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: In part I, chapter III of the Testament politique, Richelieu proposed ways to preserve the nobility as a distinct order, including giving poor nobles access to posts in which they could maintain their rank.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Richelieu’s New France charter conferred the rights of native French subjects on Indigenous people who embraced Catholicism, including rights to settle in France and hold or inherit property there.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: In the charter he signed for New France, Richelieu granted a company of associates in France exclusive rights to its fur exports and a temporary monopoly over most of its other trade.

country-wealth-only-from-land.rationale: In part II, chapter IX of the Testament politique, Richelieu describes fishing, manufactures, and maritime commerce as sources of wealth for France.

death-penalty.rationale: In part I, chapter I of the Testament politique, Richelieu recounts the executions of Marshal Marillac and the Duke of Montmorency and describes the ministers’ resistance to pleas for clemency in the latter case.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: In part II, chapter II of the Testament politique, Richelieu argued for excluding women as a rule from public administration and justified that exclusion by appealing to what he took to be inherent differences between the sexes.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: In part I, chapter I of the Testament politique, Richelieu describes the authority kings exercise over their subjects as received from heaven.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In part II, chapter V of the Testament politique, Richelieu allowed the government to imprison or remove people suspected of plotting against public safety before obtaining the proof ordinarily required.

harm-principle.rationale: In part II, chapter I of the Testament politique, Richelieu urged princes to use penal laws against irreligious speech and conduct to advance religious observance.

immigration-favours-shared-culture.rationale: Richelieu’s charter directed the company to recruit settlers for New France from native French Catholics and instructed colonial officials to enforce that restriction.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Richelieu’s charter conveyed jurisdiction and extensive authority to allocate land in New France to the Hundred Associates.

more-religion-public.rationale: Richelieu’s charter required the company to maintain at least three clergy in each settlement in New France so they could conduct ministry and seek converts.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Richelieu secured royal letters patent to establish the Académie française and charge it with developing the French language for use in the arts and sciences.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Richelieu signed the charter granting the Hundred Associates exclusive rights to the New France fur trade and temporary exclusive rights to most other commerce there.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: In part II, chapter V of the Testament politique, Richelieu permitted detention or exile based on strong suspicions in affairs of state before the evidence ordinarily required for judicial action was established.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: In part II, chapter I of the Testament politique, Richelieu urged rulers and magistrates to enforce laws that punished blasphemy severely.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The New France charter signed by Richelieu legally reserved immigration to the colony for French Catholics.

replace-appointed-officials.rationale: In part I, chapter V, section II of the Testament politique, Richelieu argued against replacing appointed governors compulsorily after three years. He thought a short term would encourage governors to extract as much private profit as they could before leaving office.

separate-church-state.rationale: The New France charter signed by Richelieu assigned colonial authorities the task of enforcing a Catholic eligibility requirement for settlers and obliged the company to finance a Catholic ministry.

separated-powers.rationale: The February 1641 edict under Richelieu reserved affairs of state and administration to the crown and required the courts to register royal edicts after the king had heard and ruled on their remonstrances.

spiritual-nature.rationale: In part II, chapter I of the Testament politique, Richelieu says princes have an obligation to seek the conversion of subjects and to promote their salvation through the means available to government.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Richelieu’s charter directed company resources into shipping and the establishment of settlements in New France and backed the effort with exclusive trading rights.

state-harmful.rationale: Richelieu recounts in part I, chapter I of the Testament politique how his ministry strengthened royal government against armed rivals and secured control of contested strongholds.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: In part II, chapter I of the Testament politique, Richelieu directs magistrates to foster religious observance through the ruler’s example and the enforcement of laws against conduct he regarded as impious.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: In part I, chapter I of the Testament politique, Richelieu recounts France’s continued subsidies and alliance with the Dutch against Spain, and its negotiations with imperial electors to thwart the Habsburgs at Regensburg.

taxation-theft.rationale: In part II, chapter IX, section VII of the Testament politique, Richelieu recognizes subjects’ legitimate dues to the sovereign and explains why reserves and taxes must leave them enough to sustain commerce.

trade-surplus.rationale: In part II, chapter IX, section VI of the Testament politique, Richelieu urged France to draw money from neighboring countries by exporting grain and other goods they needed while replacing imports it could produce itself.

women-suffrage.rationale: In part II, chapter II of the Testament politique, Richelieu argued that women should generally be excluded from public administration, admitting only individual exceptions.

notes: The review searched the Testament politique for government, religion, criminal law, education, taxation, commerce, diplomacy, and military policy, and checked the record of the Huguenot wars, the Académie française, and colonial settlement and trade. The charter concerns settlement in a specific colony. The literary academy’s mandate concerns development of French, without establishing a policy restricting minority language use. The Paris parlement was a court, so its dispute with the crown does not settle parliamentary legislative supremacy. The follow-up examined the judicial edict of 1641, colonial naturalization through conversion, claims about France’s historical domains, and the record of taxation and internal revolts. The seventeenth-century evidence concerns religious status and dynastic allegiance more directly than modern racial or nationalist doctrines.
